subject: Art & Design
title: Decision Architecture: How Layout Shapes Choices
description: A 60-second lesson on Decision Architecture: How Layout Shapes Choices.

hook.text: A cafeteria put salads at eye level and cookies on the bottom shelf. Salad sales jumped 25%. The menu didn't change.

buildup.text: Decision architecture arranges choices so the desired option becomes the easiest to pick, without removing alternatives.

discovery.text: Key techniques: defaults (opt-in vs. opt-out), ordering (first items get picked more), and framing (loss vs. gain).

twist.text: Every design is a choice architecture. There's no neutral layout — even randomization is a decision about decisions.

climax.text: Organ donation rates: Germany (opt-in) has 12% donors. Austria (opt-out) has 99.98%. Same culture, different default.

punchline.text: You can't design without influencing choices. The only choice is how.

quiz.question: What is decision architecture in design?
options: Arranging choices so the preferred option becomes the easiest to select
Removing all options except the one the designer prefers
Making all choices equally difficult to find

details.summary: Decision architecture arranges options, information, and visual elements to influence which choices people make. Column layout, option ordering, visual emphasis, and comparison tables all shape decisions by making some options easier to evaluate and select than others.
details.whyItMatters: There's no neutral way to present choices — every layout choice influences decisions. Understanding decision architecture empowers designers to present options fairly and clearly, or reveals how others may be steering choices.
takeaways: Layout and ordering influence which options users select
There is no neutral way to present a set of choices
Visual emphasis and comparison formats steer decisions

faq.question: How does option ordering affect choices?
faq.answer: Items listed first receive disproportionate attention and selection (primacy effect). Items marked as 'recommended' or 'most popular' are chosen far more often. Center-stage options in a horizontal layout get more clicks. Simply reordering identical options changes which one people choose.

faq.question: What is a decoy effect in decision architecture?
faq.answer: Adding an inferior option that's similar but clearly worse than the target makes the target look better by comparison. A cinema selling small ($3) and large ($7) popcorn adds a medium ($6.50) that makes the large seem like a bargain. The medium exists only to make the large attractive.
